title: The potential of nanosized zeolites in catalysis
content: Zeolites with well-defined microporous frameworks are among the most widely utilized heterogeneous catalysts in petroleum refining, fine chemical synthesis, and environmental protection. However, the intrinsic diffusion limitations associated with conventional micron-sized crystals often restrict catalytic efficiency, product selectivity, and catalyst lifetime, particularly in reactions involving bulky molecules. Reducing zeolite crystal dimensions to the nanoscale has emerged as an effective strategy to alleviate transport constraints, increase external surface area, and tailor the distribution and accessibility of acid sites. As a result, nanosized zeolites have attracted significant attention as advanced catalytic materials with enhanced activity, selectivity, and stability. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in nanosized zeolites, with particular emphasis on the relationship between crystal size, diffusion phenomena, acidity, and catalytic performance. The discussion is organized according to the most industrially relevant framework topologies, including 12-membered-ring zeolites (FAU, *BEA, MOR, and LTL), 10-membered-ring zeolites (MFI, FER, MWW, and MEL), and the 8-membered-ring zeolite (CHA). Each topology is critically analyzed individually, while comparative summaries are provided to highlight key structural and catalytic trends. Diverse nanoscale architectures including aggregated and monodispersed nanoparticles, self-pillared and intergrown structures, intra-crystalline mesoporous systems, finned morphologies, and nanosheets are examined to illustrate how structural design governs diffusion pathways and catalytic behavior. Particular attention is devoted to the incorporation of heteroatoms and the modulation of acidity, which play central roles in determining catalytic activity and product selectivity.
